category.name: Geospatial & Imagery
category.description: Satellite and aerial imagery, street-level photography, map data and solar geometry — the toolkit for placing an image on the earth and for establishing what was at a location on a given date. Most geolocation work is done with these tools plus patience.

tools.name: Google Earth Pro
tools.summary: Desktop globe with a historical imagery slider, measurement tools and 3D terrain — the workhorse of geolocation.
tools.description:
Google Earth Pro is the desktop application, and the reason it matters more than the web version is the historical imagery timeline. You can step backwards through years of archived satellite and aerial captures of the same place, which is how you establish when a building appeared, when a road was paved, or which of several candidate locations matches a photograph taken in a particular year.

It also provides the measurement tools that make geolocation rigorous rather than impressionistic: ruler measurements between features, elevation profiles, and 3D terrain that lets you compare a ridgeline in a photograph against the modelled horizon.

Limits: imagery dates and resolution vary enormously by location, with wealthy urban areas updated often and rural areas in some regions barely covered. The date shown on an image is the capture date Google records, which is usually right but is not itself independently verifiable from within the tool. 3D building models are reconstructions and are not reliable for fine detail.
tools.costNotes: Google Earth Pro for desktop has been free since 2015, when Google discontinued the paid licence. No payment or subscription is required; a Google account is not needed for basic use.
tools.legalNotes: Viewing is unrestricted, but reuse is not: Google's imagery is licensed and republishing a screenshot in a commercial product or a report may require attribution and may exceed permitted use. Check the current Google Earth and Maps attribution guidelines before publishing. Note also that in a handful of jurisdictions the collection or publication of detailed imagery of specific sites is restricted by national law.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The imagery itself is a faithful capture, and the historical archive is the single most useful geolocation asset available for free. Capture dates should be treated as accurate but not independently verified. Imagery is sometimes stitched from passes on different dates, which can put two inconsistent states in one view — a classic trap when dating a change. Corroborate any date-critical conclusion against a second imagery source.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established and stable; the free status of Earth Pro has held since 2015. Not fetched during this review.

tools.name: Copernicus Browser
tools.summary: Free browser access to the full Sentinel satellite archive with band combinations, comparison and download.
tools.description:
The Copernicus Browser is the EU's official access point to Sentinel imagery within the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem. It replaced Sentinel Hub's EO Browser, which is now deprecated and redirects users here; the Copernicus Browser is built on that same open-source codebase.

For investigations it does something Google Earth cannot: it gives you a dated, regularly repeating optical and radar archive that you can query for a specific day. Sentinel-2 optical imagery revisits every few days at 10-metre resolution, and Sentinel-1 radar sees through cloud and at night. That combination is how open-source analysts date events — a burn scar, a new revetment, a ship at a berth, a flooded area — to a window of days.

Band combinations matter and are its real power: false-colour, NDVI and SWIR composites reveal vegetation loss, burn scars, moisture and thermal anomalies that are invisible in true colour. Limits: 10-metre resolution shows that something changed, not what it is. You cannot identify a vehicle or a person. Cloud cover defeats optical imagery, and radar takes practice to interpret without over-reading.
tools.costNotes: Free and open. Sentinel data can be viewed anonymously without logging in; a free Copernicus Data Space account is needed for downloads and some advanced functions. The underlying Copernicus data is published under a free, full and open licence.
tools.legalNotes: Copernicus data is published under an open licence permitting reuse including commercial use, with attribution — one of the cleanest licensing positions of any imagery source in this catalogue. Confirm the current attribution wording before publication.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Authoritative, systematically collected, precisely dated public-sector imagery with documented processing levels. The constraints are physical rather than editorial: 10-metre optical resolution limits what can be identified, cloud blocks optical passes, and radar interpretation is genuinely difficult and easy to get wrong. Analysts routinely over-interpret low-resolution pixels — state what the resolution can actually support.
tools.confidenceNotes: Confirmed during this review that EO Browser is deprecated in favour of the Copernicus Browser at the URL given, that the Copernicus Browser derives from the EO Browser codebase, and that Sentinel-2 data can be viewed without logging in.

tools.name: USGS EarthExplorer
tools.summary: US Geological Survey portal to Landsat, aerial photography and declassified satellite archives going back decades.
tools.description:
EarthExplorer is the access point for the USGS archives, and its distinguishing asset is depth of time. Landsat has been imaging the earth continuously since 1972. Declassified US reconnaissance imagery from the Corona, Argon and Lanyard programmes covers parts of the world from the 1960s. Historical aerial photography covers much of the United States from the mid-twentieth century.

When the question is what was here before, this is often the only answer available. Documenting the destruction of a village, the historical extent of a lake, or the original footprint of a site that has since been redeveloped depends on archives of this age, and no commercial provider goes back that far.

Limits: the interface is dated and the search is unforgiving. Landsat's 30-metre resolution is coarse — it shows landscape change, not objects. Declassified imagery is film-scanned, geometrically distorted and requires georeferencing work before it can be compared to a modern map. Coverage outside the US thins considerably for the aerial collections.
tools.costNotes: Free. Browsing and searching require no account, but downloading data requires a free USGS ERS account. Some third-party collections hosted in the interface carry their own restrictions.
tools.legalNotes: USGS-produced data is generally in the US public domain and freely reusable, which makes it excellent for publication. Not everything reachable through EarthExplorer is USGS-produced — some hosted collections come from commercial or partner sources with their own licences. Check the specific dataset's terms before republishing.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Authoritative government archives with precise acquisition metadata. The practical difficulty is handling rather than trust: declassified film products need georeferencing and their nominal coordinates can be substantially off, and Landsat's resolution supports landscape-scale conclusions only. Do not assert object-level detail from 30-metre pixels.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established government service. Not fetched during this review; USGS has reorganised its data portals several times, so confirm the current entry point.

tools.name: NASA Worldview
tools.summary: Browse near-real-time full-earth satellite imagery by date, with hundreds of scientific overlay layers.
tools.description:
Worldview presents NASA's Earth observation holdings as a date-driven global browser. You pick a day and see the earth as the satellites saw it, with several hundred selectable layers: true and false colour, aerosol and smoke, fire detections, sea surface temperature, snow and ice, night lights.

Its value in investigations is speed and coverage on a specific date. It answers questions like whether there was smoke over a region on a particular morning, whether cloud would have obscured a claimed observation, or whether a dust storm was in progress — all useful for testing or corroborating an account of an event.

Limits: most layers are at moderate to coarse resolution, typically hundreds of metres to a kilometre per pixel. This is the wrong tool for anything site-specific. It tells you about atmospheric and regional conditions, not about a building.
tools.costNotes: Free, no account required, with imagery served through open NASA GIBS services that can be used programmatically.
tools.legalNotes: NASA imagery is generally free to use with attribution and is well suited to publication. Confirm any specific dataset's citation requirement, as some layers come from partner agencies with their own terms.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Authoritative scientific data with clear provenance and dating. The near-real-time layers are exactly that — provisional products that are later reprocessed, so a NRT observation may differ slightly from the final science product. Resolution is the binding constraint; do not read site-level detail into kilometre-scale pixels.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established, stable NASA service. Not fetched during this review.

tools.name: NASA FIRMS
tools.summary: Near-real-time satellite detections of active fires and thermal anomalies, globally, within hours.
tools.description:
The Fire Information for Resource Management System distributes active fire and thermal-anomaly detections from MODIS aboard the Aqua and Terra satellites and from VIIRS aboard Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. Detections are published globally within about three hours of observation, and in real time for the United States and Canada.

For conflict and environmental investigation this is a workhorse. Thermal detections corroborate reports of shelling, airstrikes, industrial fires, gas flaring and the burning of villages or crops, with a timestamp and coordinates you can cross-reference against imagery and witness accounts. Detections are downloadable as points with confidence values, so they integrate directly into mapping.

The limits are important and routinely ignored. A detection means the sensor saw a thermal anomaly of sufficient intensity in a pixel of several hundred metres — it does not say what burned or why. Gas flares, industrial plant, agricultural burning and wildfire all register. Cloud hides fires, and a satellite only sees a location on its overpass, so a short fire between passes leaves no trace. A FIRMS point is corroboration, never proof of a specific event.
tools.costNotes: Free. Map browsing needs no account. Data is downloadable as SHP, KML, TXT and via WMS, and email alerts are offered. A free key is required for some programmatic access.
tools.legalNotes: NASA public data, freely usable with attribution. No subject notification and no access restrictions of note.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The detections are reliable as detections and carry explicit confidence values that should be reported alongside any use. What they are not is an interpretation: attributing a detection to a particular cause requires independent evidence. Known false positives include industrial heat sources and sun glint. Spatial precision is limited by pixel size, so a detection locates an event to within hundreds of metres, not to a building.
tools.confidenceNotes: Fetched during this review: live, with the MODIS and VIIRS instrument set, the three-hour global near-real-time latency and the US/Canada real-time availability confirmed from the site.

tools.name: OpenStreetMap
tools.summary: Open, editable world map whose full underlying data and complete edit history are downloadable.
tools.description:
OpenStreetMap is a crowd-built geographic database covering roads, buildings, land use, waterways, addresses and points of interest. Unlike commercial maps, the underlying data is open — every object, its tags, and the complete history of who changed what and when.

That history is an investigative source in itself. You can see when a feature was added, by which account, and what it was before. For rapidly changing environments, OSM is often updated by local contributors faster than any commercial provider.

Coverage is uneven in exactly the way volunteer data always is: superb in well-mapped cities, sparse in areas without an active local community, and occasionally subject to vandalism or well-meaning error. It is a map that must be checked against imagery before you rely on it, and its greatest use in geolocation is not the rendered map but querying its tags — which is what Overpass Turbo is for.
tools.costNotes: Free to view and use. Data is licensed under the Open Database Licence, which is a share-alike licence with real obligations on derived databases. Editing requires a free account.
tools.legalNotes: The ODbL is not public domain. Attribution is required, and producing and publishing a derived database can trigger share-alike obligations — a genuine and commonly overlooked constraint if you build a product on OSM data. Read the licence before commercial reuse. Contributor account names and edit histories are public.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Excellent where the local mapping community is active and thin where it is not, with no indication in the map itself of which situation you are in. Vandalism happens and is usually reverted quickly but can be live when you look. Always verify a critical OSM feature against imagery or ground-level photography before basing a geolocation on it.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established global project. Not fetched during this review.

tools.name: Overpass Turbo
tools.summary: Query interface to OpenStreetMap data — find every feature matching a set of tags within an area.
tools.description:
Overpass Turbo is a web front-end to the Overpass API, which queries the OpenStreetMap database directly. Instead of looking at a map, you ask it questions: every water tower within this bounding box, every mosque within 5 km of this point, every football pitch adjacent to a railway.

This is the single most powerful geolocation technique available for free, and it is underused because it requires learning a query syntax. The method is simple: extract distinctive features from a photograph — a stadium, a distinctive road junction, a wind farm, a chimney, a body of water of a particular shape — and query for places where that combination co-occurs. A search space of a whole country collapses to a handful of candidates you can check by hand.

Limits: it can only find what is tagged. An unmapped feature is invisible, and tagging conventions vary by region and mapper, so a query that works in Germany may return nothing in a less-mapped country for reasons that have nothing to do with the feature's existence. A null result is never evidence of absence.
tools.costNotes: Free, no account. It runs against public Overpass API instances that are volunteer-funded and rate-limited; heavy or badly written queries will be throttled, and running your own instance is the answer for sustained work.
tools.legalNotes: Results are OpenStreetMap data and carry the same ODbL attribution and share-alike obligations. The public Overpass endpoints are a shared community resource — writing unbounded or repetitive queries degrades them for everyone, and respecting their rate limits is both the terms of use and basic courtesy.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The query returns exactly what OSM contains, faithfully — so its reliability is OSM's reliability plus your query's correctness. Most apparent failures are query errors or tagging assumptions, not missing data. Before concluding a feature does not exist anywhere in a region, verify your query returns known instances of that feature in the same region.
tools.confidenceNotes: Fetched during this review and confirmed live and functioning as an Overpass API front-end over OpenStreetMap data.

tools.name: Mapillary
tools.summary: Crowdsourced street-level imagery covering places commercial street view does not reach.
tools.description:
Mapillary hosts street-level photography contributed by volunteers, mapping agencies and organisations, with a reported corpus in the billions of images. It has been owned by Meta since 2020 and remains actively developed, with API changes shipped through 2026.

Its investigative value is filling the gaps in Google Street View. Roads, tracks, informal settlements and whole countries that commercial street-view vehicles never covered are often present in Mapillary because someone drove or walked them with a phone or an action camera. For geolocation in under-covered regions it is frequently the only ground-level imagery available.

Limits: coverage is entirely a function of who bothered, so it is dense along some routes and absent a street away. Image quality ranges from professional survey rigs to shaky phone footage. Crucially, each image carries a capture date that you must read — it is easy to match a photograph against Mapillary imagery from a different year and mistake a change for a mismatch.
tools.costNotes: Viewing imagery is free. A developer API is available and has continued to receive updates through 2026; access terms and any usage limits are set by Mapillary and were not verified in this review.
tools.legalNotes: Imagery is contributed under Mapillary's terms and reuse conditions have changed over the platform's history — confirm the current licence before republishing an image, and do not assume it is freely reusable. The imagery contains incidentally captured people and vehicle plates; Mapillary applies automated blurring, but it is imperfect, and publishing a crop containing an identifiable uninvolved person is your decision and your exposure.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Faithful ground-level imagery with location and date metadata. Positional accuracy depends on the contributor's GPS and can be tens of metres off, particularly in urban canyons — do not treat a Mapillary point as a survey-grade coordinate. Coverage gaps are the main practical limit and give no signal about what is there.
tools.confidenceNotes: Confirmed during this review as active in 2026, with API changes documented in early 2026 and continued platform activity. Meta's 2020 acquisition confirmed. Licensing terms for reuse were not verified.

tools.name: KartaView
tools.summary: Open street-level imagery platform, an alternative and complement to Mapillary with different coverage.
tools.description:
KartaView (formerly OpenStreetCam) is a crowdsourced street-level imagery platform closely associated with the OpenStreetMap community. Contributors upload sequences captured from vehicles and the imagery is made available for viewing and, importantly, for improving OSM.

It earns a place alongside Mapillary for one reason: different contributors chose different platforms, so coverage differs. A road with no Mapillary imagery may have KartaView sequences and vice versa. When ground-level imagery is the missing link in a geolocation, checking both roughly doubles your chance of finding it.

Its corpus is smaller than Mapillary's and its coverage is concentrated where its contributor community has been active, with notable density in parts of Europe. The same date-reading discipline applies.
tools.costNotes: Free to view and contribute. Historically positioned as an open imagery platform aligned with the OpenStreetMap community; current licence terms were not verified in this review.
tools.legalNotes: Confirm the current image licence before republishing. As with any street-level imagery, uninvolved people and vehicle registrations are incidentally captured; blurring is applied but is not perfect, and publication decisions about identifiable third parties are yours.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Reliable for what it holds, but coverage is substantially thinner and more geographically concentrated than Mapillary, and contribution activity has varied over the platform's life. Positional accuracy is GPS-dependent and imprecise. Useful as a complement, not a primary source.
tools.confidenceNotes: The platform is real and has a long history under two names, but its current level of activity, corpus size, operator and licence terms were not verified during this review. Confirm it is live before relying on it in a workflow.

tools.name: SunCalc
tools.summary: Calculates the sun's position and shadow direction for any location, date and time — the standard tool for chronolocation.
tools.description:
SunCalc shows, for a given point on a map and a given date and time, where the sun is in the sky: its azimuth, its elevation, sunrise and sunset times, and the direction and relative length of shadows.

This is how you date a photograph. Shadows in an image encode the sun's position at the moment of capture. If you know where the photograph was taken and can measure a shadow's direction and its ratio to the height of the object casting it, SunCalc tells you the times of day at which that geometry occurs, and — because the sun's path changes through the year — narrows the possible dates. Running the process in reverse tests a claimed time and place against physics.

The method has hard limits that must be stated in any finding. The sun's position repeats: any given shadow angle occurs on two dates a year and often at two times a day, so chronolocation yields a set of candidate windows, not a single answer. Accuracy depends entirely on how precisely you can measure the shadow and how confident you are in the location. Overcast conditions, ambiguous shadow edges and unknown terrain slope all degrade it. Used honestly it excludes far more than it confirms — and exclusion is a real result.
tools.costNotes: Free to use in a browser with no account.
tools.legalNotes: Purely computational tool operating on astronomical data; it involves no personal data and no interaction with any subject.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The underlying solar-position calculation is astronomy and is accurate. Every error in practice comes from the analyst's inputs: an imprecise location, a misread shadow, a wrong assumption about the local time zone or daylight saving, or terrain that is not flat. State your uncertainty in the output explicitly — a chronolocation result should always be expressed as a range with reasoning, never a single timestamp.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established, widely used free tool. Not fetched during this review; other implementations of the same calculation exist if it is unavailable.
